thread.title: Groups argue against repaying court-appointed attorney fees - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: Groups argue against repaying court-appointed attorney fees - NewsBreak

author: Sharon Wren
title: Groups argue against repaying court-appointed attorney fees - NewsBreak
text:
By Sharon Wren ,
7 hours ago
The Iowa Supreme Court heard arguments this morning in a case that would force Iowa courts to stop charging low-income Iowans for the costs of their court-appointed defense attorneys when criminal charges against them have been dismissed.
Public Justice, the Fines and Fees Justice Center and the ACLU of Iowa filed an amicus brief in the case of State of Iowa v. Ronald Pagliai. Attorneys presented their oral arguments at the Iowa Supreme Court building in Des Moines.
The groups held a Zoom press conference after the hearing to discuss the case. Alex Kornya, cooperating attorney with the ACLU of Iowa, gave background into the filing. “This is actually the second time the Iowa Supreme Court has addressed the issue of whether or not someone can be assessed costs in a criminal case, despite the fact that they were never found guilty of any crime.
“The first time this issue reached the Iowa Supreme Court was in 2020 in a case called State versus Mathis and the ACLU, Fines and Fees Justice Center and Iowa Legal Aid filed an amicus back in 2020,” he said. “One justice, Justice McDermott, newly appointed, recused, leaving us with no decision, and the underlying decision of the Iowa Court of Appeals affirmed by operation of law. The practice of assessing, oftentimes hundreds, if not thousands of dollars to people in cases that did not result in any type of finding of guilt, continued in the state of Iowa for another five years, until the court revisited the issue in an argument that was heard earlier this morning.”
“The filing says there is no statute in the Iowa Code that would allow for these debts to be assessed, a position with which the state, in fact, did not disagree. The state’s position was that prior case law of the court would justify this, but we all agreed that there is nothing in the Iowa Code that would allow for these types of debts to be assessed. We also, in our briefing, extensively talked about several reasons why, even if there was a statute that would allow for debts to be assessed against someone in a criminal case without a finding of guilt, those debts would not be constitutionally issued.”
“When we’re talking about these types of debts, we’re talking about primarily debts that are assessed against low-income people, to repay the state for the cost of defense,” Kornya said. “There are some smaller costs here and there, like filing fees that apply to everyone across the board, but by and large, the lion’s share of the debt that we were talking about only applies to some criminal defendants, specifically people who do not have the money to hire their own attorney.”
“In return for exercising the constitutional right to an attorney to defend them in a criminal case, they are charged actual cost. In the state of Iowa, many states have what are called recoupment statutes that allow the states to collect back at least some of what is expended on the cost of their defense. But Iowa really stands out because, again, it’s actual cost, which a lot of states it’s capped. These debts can be assessed against people, even if they win their case. That is unusual.”
Kornya says the rate of collecting on these assessments is extremely low. “Between 2017 and 2021, statistics published by the Judicial branch to the Iowa legislature show that the collection rate was between 1 and 2%, which is effectively zero. One of the things that we found to be, I think, particularly perverse about the assessment of these debts in dismissed cases is that, at least for convictions and acquittals, that people have a right to reduce the amount they owe based on their ability to pay. When someone has a dismissed case, they bypass that ability to pay determination. So, it’s not even as simple as saying that people who have dismissed cases are in the same position as someone who is convicted. They’re actually in a worse position and often end up owing more for their case than they would have if they had been convicted, which makes no sense.”
The Iowa Supreme Court is considering the brief, but there is no timeline for a decision.
